claim: Brain tissues rarely fossilize.
source: Because brain tissues rarely fossilize, pinpointing when and how modern human cerebral traits emerged in the hominin lineage is particularly challenging.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the fossilization process and preservation of soft tissues.

claim: Pinpointing when and how modern human cerebral traits emerged in the hominin lineage is particularly challenging.
source: Because brain tissues rarely fossilize, pinpointing when and how modern human cerebral traits emerged in the hominin lineage is particularly challenging.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the rarity of brain tissue fossilization and the fragmentary nature of fossil material mentioned in the text.

claim: The fragmentary nature of the fossil material has been the source of long-standing debates.
source: The fragmentary nature of the fossil material, coupled with the difficulty of characterizing such a complex organ, has been the source of long-standing debates.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the state of paleoanthropological research and its challenges.

claim: The difficulty of characterizing the brain has been the source of long-standing debates.
source: The fragmentary nature of the fossil material, coupled with the difficulty of characterizing such a complex organ, has been the source of long-standing debates.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the complexity of brain characterization in paleoanthropology.

claim: There are uncertainties around the derived or primitive state of the brain organization in the earliest representatives of the genus Homo.
source: Prominent among them are the uncertainties around the derived or primitive state of the brain organization in the earliest representatives of the genus Homo, more particularly in key regions such as the Broca's area.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ongoing debates in paleoanthropology.

claim: Early Homo in Africa had a primitive organization of the Broca's area ca. 1.9 million years ago.
source: By revisiting a particularly well-preserved fossil endocast from the Turkana basin (Kenya), here we confirm that early Homo in Africa had a primitive organization of the Broca's area ca. 1.9 million years ago.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of KNM-ER 3732 presented in the manuscript.

claim: The description of KNM-ER 3732 adds information about the variation pattern of the inferior frontal gyrus in fossil hominins.
source: Additionally, our description of KNM-ER 3732 adds further information about the variation pattern of the inferior frontal gyrus in fossil hominins, with implications for early Homo taxic diversity (i.e. one or two Homo species at Koobi Fora) and the nature of the mechanisms involved in the emergence of derived cerebral traits.
evidence: This is based on the comparative analysis of KNM-ER 3732 presented in the manuscript.

claim: The modern human brain is an exceptionally complex, highly specialized, and extremely costly machinery.
source: The modern human brain is an exceptionally complex, highly specialized, and extremely costly machinery.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about human brain characteristics.

claim: Assessing when and how changes in the brain of our ancestors happened is particularly challenging because of the fragmentary nature of the hominin fossil record.
source: Because of the fragmentary nature of the hominin fossil record, assessing when and how changes in the brain of our ancestors happened, and inferring any related functional, behavioral, and metabolic consequences, is particularly challenging (Zollikofer and De León, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zollikofer and De León, 2013.

claim: Reconstructing the chronological and taxonomical context of the emergence of derived cerebral traits is a prerequisite for disentangling underlying evolutionary processes.
source: Nonetheless, reconstructing the chronological and taxonomical context of the emergence of derived cerebral traits is a prerequisite for disentangling underlying evolutionary processes.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the requirements for understanding evolutionary processes.

claim: Local reorganization of specific areas in an overall primitive hominin brain would support a mosaic-like evolutionary pattern.
source: For instance, local reorganization of specific areas in an overall primitive hominin brain would support a mosaic-like evolutionary pattern (e.g. Holloway et al., 2004), and raise essential questions on the role of selection pressure (or absence of; rev. in Beaudet, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Holloway et al., 2004 and Beaudet, 2021.

claim: It is possible to glean structural information about the evolutionary history of the hominin brain by studying sulcal imprints in fossil brain endocasts.
source: Although brains rarely fossilize, it is possible to glean structural information about the evolutionary history of the hominin brain by studying sulcal imprints in fossil brain endocasts (Neubauer, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Neubauer, 2014.

claim: The Broca's area has been the focus of much interest in paleoneurology due to striking structural differences between extant human and chimpanzee brains and endocasts.
source: In this regard, the Broca's area has been the focus of much interest in paleoneurology due to striking structural differences between extant human and chimpanzee brains and endocasts, and the implication of this area in articulated language (rev. in Beaudet, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Beaudet, 2017.

claim: The Broca's area has been the focus of much interest in paleoneurology due to the implication of this area in articulated language.
source: In this regard, the Broca's area has been the focus of much interest in paleoneurology due to striking structural differences between extant human and chimpanzee brains and endocasts, and the implication of this area in articulated language (rev. in Beaudet, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Beaudet, 2017.

claim: Ponce de León et al., 2021 demonstrated that the organization of the Broca's area in the earliest representatives of the genus before 1.5 Ma was primitive.
source: Ponce de León et al., 2021 thoroughly examined brain endocasts of Homo specimens in eastern Africa and Eurasia and demonstrated that the organization of the Broca's area in the earliest representatives of the genus before 1.5 Ma was primitive.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ponce de León et al., 2021.

claim: Ponce de León et al., 2021 used the coronal suture and surrounding sulcal imprints as a proxy to identify frontal lobe expansion.
source: Because the imprints of the Broca's cap in endocasts are not always readable, they used the coronal suture and surrounding sulcal imprints as a proxy to identify frontal lobe expansion (i.e. derived condition).
evidence: This is based on the cited work of Ponce de León et al., 2021.

claim: In some of the oldest and key specimens from Africa that could represent the >1.5 Ma condition (e.g. KNM-ER 1470) the interpretations remained inconclusive.
source: Unfortunately, in some of the oldest and key specimens from Africa that could represent the >1.5 Ma condition (e.g. KNM-ER 1470) the interpretations remained inconclusive.
evidence: This is based on the cited work of Ponce de León et al., 2021.

claim: KNM-ER 3732 has the potential to shed new light on the conundrum of brain organization in early Homo.
source: The hominin specimen KNM-ER 3732 from Kenya, which fulfills these requirements, has the potential to shed new light on this conundrum.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential contribution of the specimen.

claim: KNM-ER 3732 was discovered during the 1974–1975 field program in the Koobi Fora Formation (area 115), east of Lake Turkana in Kenya.
source: KNM-ER 3732 was discovered during the 1974–1975 field program in the Koobi Fora Formation (area 115), east of Lake Turkana in Kenya (Leakey, 1976; Wood, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Leakey, 1976 and Wood, 1991.

claim: KNM-ER 3732 consists of a calotte, left zygoma, and a natural endocast.
source: KNM-ER 3732 consists of a calotte, left zygoma, and a natural endocast.
evidence: This is a direct observation of the specimen composition.

claim: The expanded neurocranium and robust upper face support an attribution to Homo sp. indet.
source: The expanded neurocranium and robust upper face support an attribution to Homo sp. indet. (Wood, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wood, 1991.

claim: The specimen was lying below the KBS Tuff of the upper Burgi Member that is dated to 1.87 million years ago.
source: The specimen was lying below the KBS Tuff of the upper Burgi Member that is dated to 1.87 million years ago, which provides a minimum age (Feibel et al., 1983; Feibel et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Feibel et al., 1983 and Feibel et al., 2006.

claim: The stratigraphic position of KNM-ER 3732 provides a minimum age of 1.87 million years ago.
source: The specimen was lying below the KBS Tuff of the upper Burgi Member that is dated to 1.87 million years ago, which provides a minimum age (Feibel et al., 1983; Feibel et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an inference based on stratigraphic principles and supported by citations.

claim: If KNM-ER 3732 shows a derived cerebral condition, the hypothesis of >1.5 Ma Homo being associated with a primitive organization of the Broca's area is falsified.
source: Accordingly, if KNM-ER 3732 shows a derived cerebral condition, the hypothesis of >1.5 Ma Homo being associated with a primitive organization of the Broca's area is falsified.
evidence: This is a logical inference about hypothesis testing.

claim: The natural endocast of KNM-ER 3732 was initially described by Holloway et al., 2004.
source: The natural endocast of KNM-ER 3732, initially described by Holloway et al., 2004, preserves the dorsal part but misses the frontal pole, the occipital and temporal lobes, as well as the entire ventral surface (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Holloway et al., 2004.

claim: The natural endocast of KNM-ER 3732 preserves the dorsal part but misses the frontal pole, the occipital and temporal lobes, as well as the entire ventral surface.
source: The natural endocast of KNM-ER 3732, initially described by Holloway et al., 2004, preserves the dorsal part but misses the frontal pole, the occipital and temporal lobes, as well as the entire ventral surface (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on direct observation of the specimen and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Holloway et al., 2004 estimated the endocranial volume as about 750–800 cc.
source: Holloway et al., 2004 estimated the endocranial volume as about 750–800 cc but pointed out the low reliability of their estimate.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Holloway et al., 2004.

claim: Holloway et al., 2004 pointed out the low reliability of their endocranial volume estimate for KNM-ER 3732.
source: Holloway et al., 2004 estimated the endocranial volume as about 750–800 cc but pointed out the low reliability of their estimate.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Holloway et al., 2004.

claim: Wood, 1991 identified an irregular bony excrescence on the surface of the right parietal at the level of lambda and 32 mm from the midline.
source: Wood, 1991 (Page 132) identified an 'irregular bony excrescence on the surface of the right parietal at the level of lambda and 32 mm from the midline. It projects 6 mm from the surface of the bone, and may be an example of myositis ossificans associated with damage to the overlying temporal muscle.'
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wood, 1991.

claim: The bony excrescence on KNM-ER 3732 may be an example of myositis ossificans associated with damage to the overlying temporal muscle.
source: Wood, 1991 (Page 132) identified an 'irregular bony excrescence on the surface of the right parietal at the level of lambda and 32 mm from the midline. It projects 6 mm from the surface of the bone, and may be an example of myositis ossificans associated with damage to the overlying temporal muscle.'
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation by Wood, 1991.

claim: The bony outgrowth does not affect the area of study (i.e. left frontal bone) because of its location (right parietal) and nature (traumatic).
source: Because of the location (right parietal) and nature (traumatic) of the outgrowth, it does not affect our area of study (i.e. left frontal bone) (Walczak et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical location and supported by citation to Walczak et al., 2015.

claim: The gyral and sulcal details are well-preserved in KNM-ER 3732, particularly in the prefrontal region.
source: The gyral and sulcal details are well-preserved, particularly in the prefrontal region.
evidence: This is based on direct observation of the specimen.

claim: The superior, middle, and inferior frontal sulci are visible on both hemispheres of KNM-ER 3732.
source: The superior, middle, and inferior frontal sulci are visible on both hemispheres.
evidence: This is based on direct observation of the specimen.

claim: On the left hemisphere of KNM-ER 3732, the Broca's cap is prominent.
source: On the left hemisphere, the Broca's cap is prominent.
evidence: This is based on direct observation of the specimen.

claim: A vertical groove, identified as the precentral sulcus, separates the Broca's cap in half in KNM-ER 3732.
source: A vertical groove, identified as the precentral sulcus, separates the Broca's cap in half (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on direct observation of the specimen and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: On both hemispheres of KNM-ER 3732, the central sulcus intersects the inter-hemispheric scissure.
source: On both hemispheres, the central sulcus intersects the inter-hemispheric scissure and the post-central sulcus seems to be connected to the lateral fissure.
evidence: This is based on direct observation of the specimen.

claim: The post-central sulcus seems to be connected to the lateral fissure in KNM-ER 3732.
source: On both hemispheres, the central sulcus intersects the inter-hemispheric scissure and the post-central sulcus seems to be connected to the lateral fissure.
evidence: This is based on direct observation of the specimen.

claim: The intra-parietal sulcus can be found in the parieto-occipital region of both hemispheres of KNM-ER 3732.
source: The intra-parietal sulcus can be found in the parieto-occipital region of both hemispheres.
evidence: This is based on direct observation of the specimen.

claim: The examination of the internal surface of the braincase confirms the pattern described on the natural endocast of KNM-ER 3732.
source: The examination of the internal surface of the braincase (Figure 2B) confirms the pattern described on the natural endocast.
evidence: This is based on direct observation and comparison shown in Figure 2B.

claim: KNM-ER 3732 closely resembles the chimpanzee sulcal pattern when compared to extant human and chimpanzee sulcal patterns.
source: When compared to extant human and chimpanzee sulcal patterns, KNM-ER 3732 closely resembles the latter (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: In extant human brains and endocasts, the inferior frontal sulcus often transects the Broca's cap.
source: In extant human brains and endocasts, the inferior frontal sulcus often transects the Broca's cap, while the ascending ramus of the lateral fissure caudally borders the prominence (Figure 2C–D; Connolly, 1950; de Jager et al., 2019; de Jager et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Connolly, 1950; de Jager et al., 2019; de Jager et al., 2022 and shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: In extant human brains and endocasts, the ascending ramus of the lateral fissure caudally borders the Broca's cap prominence.
source: In extant human brains and endocasts, the inferior frontal sulcus often transects the Broca's cap, while the ascending ramus of the lateral fissure caudally borders the prominence (Figure 2C–D; Connolly, 1950; de Jager et al., 2019; de Jager et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Connolly, 1950; de Jager et al., 2019; de Jager et al., 2022 and shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: In chimpanzees, the central sulcus is placed more rostrally.
source: In chimpanzees, the central sulcus is placed more rostrally, and the inferior portion of the precentral sulcus bisects the Broca's cap that is bordered rostrally by the inferior frontal sulcus (Figure 2E–F; Connolly, 1950; Falk et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Connolly, 1950 and Falk et al., 2018 and shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: In chimpanzees, the inferior portion of the precentral sulcus bisects the Broca's cap.
source: In chimpanzees, the central sulcus is placed more rostrally, and the inferior portion of the precentral sulcus bisects the Broca's cap that is bordered rostrally by the inferior frontal sulcus (Figure 2E–F; Connolly, 1950; Falk et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Connolly, 1950 and Falk et al., 2018 and shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: In chimpanzees, the Broca's cap is bordered rostrally by the inferior frontal sulcus.
source: In chimpanzees, the central sulcus is placed more rostrally, and the inferior portion of the precentral sulcus bisects the Broca's cap that is bordered rostrally by the inferior frontal sulcus (Figure 2E–F; Connolly, 1950; Falk et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Connolly, 1950 and Falk et al., 2018 and shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: The coronal suture runs in between the precentral and central sulci in KNM-ER 3732.
source: The coronal suture runs in between the precentral and central sulci in KNM-ER 3732, which points towards the primitive configuration described in Ponce de León et al., 2021.
evidence: This is based on direct observation of the specimen.

claim: The position of the coronal suture in KNM-ER 3732 points towards the primitive configuration described in Ponce de León et al., 2021.
source: The coronal suture runs in between the precentral and central sulci in KNM-ER 3732, which points towards the primitive configuration described in Ponce de León et al., 2021.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with the work of Ponce de León et al., 2021.

claim: The deeply marked precentral sulcus that incised the Broca's cap in KNM-ER 3732 is not found in any of the early Homo specimens described in Ponce de León et al., 2021.
source: The sulcal pattern seen in the prefrontal cortex of KNM-ER 3732, that was detected in both the natural endocast and the inner surface of the cranium (Figure 2A–B), and more particularly the deeply marked precentral sulcus that incised the Broca's cap, is not found in any of the early Homo specimens described in Ponce de León et al., 2021 but approximates the condition seen in the Dmanisi cranium D2282 (Fig. S1B in Ponce de León et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis with specimens described in Ponce de León et al., 2021.

claim: The sulcal pattern in KNM-ER 3732 approximates the condition seen in the Dmanisi cranium D2282.
source: The sulcal pattern seen in the prefrontal cortex of KNM-ER 3732, that was detected in both the natural endocast and the inner surface of the cranium (Figure 2A–B), and more particularly the deeply marked precentral sulcus that incised the Broca's cap, is not found in any of the early Homo specimens described in Ponce de León et al., 2021 but approximates the condition seen in the Dmanisi cranium D2282 (Fig. S1B in Ponce de León et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis with specimens described in Ponce de León et al., 2021.

claim: The sulcal pattern in KNM-ER 3732 is seen in a contemporaneous non-Homo hominin specimen in South Africa, i.e. Australopithecus sediba.
source: However, this pattern is seen in a contemporaneous non-Homo hominin specimen in South Africa, i.e. Australopithecus sediba (Falk, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Falk, 2014.

claim: The present study demonstrates that Ponce de León et al.'s (2021) hypothesis of a primitive brain of early Homo cannot be rejected.
source: Overall, the present study not only demonstrates that Ponce de León et al.'s (2021) hypothesis of a primitive brain of early Homo cannot be rejected, but also adds information about the variation pattern of the inferior frontal gyrus.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of KNM-ER 3732 presented in the manuscript.

claim: The diversity of the prefrontal sulcal patterns of hominin endocasts at Koobi Fora revives the debate about the possible presence of two early Homo species in this locality.
source: In particular, the diversity of the prefrontal sulcal patterns of hominin endocasts at Koobi Fora revives the debate about the possible presence of two early Homo species in this locality (i.e. Homo habilis sensu stricto and Homo rudolfensis).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed variation in the specimens.

claim: In 1983, Falk, 1983 published the description of the endocasts of two Homo specimens from Koobi Fora, KNM-ER 1470 and KNM-ER 1805.
source: In 1983, Falk, 1983 published the description of the endocasts of two Homo specimens from Koobi Fora, KNM-ER 1470 and KNM-ER 1805.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Falk, 1983.

claim: Falk's (1983) analysis supported the co-existence of two morphs, with KNM-ER 1470 representing a more derived human-like sulcal pattern.
source: Her analysis supported the co-existence of two morphs, KNM-ER 1470 representing a more derived human-like sulcal pattern.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Falk, 1983.

claim: Cerebral evidence from Falk's (1983) analysis matched other studies that emphasized the more derived craniodental anatomy of specimens attributed to Homo rudolfensis.
source: Interestingly, cerebral evidence brought up by her analysis matched other studies that emphasized the more derived craniodental anatomy of specimens attributed to Homo rudolfensis as opposed to the more primitive (Australopithecus-like) traits identified within Homo habilis sensu stricto (Leakey et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Leakey et al., 2012.

claim: Leakey, 1976 noted that KNM-ER 3732 was 'strikingly similar to KNM-ER 1470' when describing the external morphology of the neurocranium.
source: While describing the external morphology of the neurocranium, (Leakey, 1976: 575) noted that KNM-ER 3732 was 'strikingly similar to KNM-ER 1470.'
evidence: This is supported by citation to Leakey, 1976.

claim: The resemblance between KNM-ER 3732 and KNM-ER 1470 in external neurocranial morphology is not reflected in their cerebral organization.
source: This resemblance is not reflected in their cerebral organization since the present study rather suggests a primitive organization of the Broca's cap in KNM-ER 3732.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of KNM-ER 3732 presented in the manuscript.

claim: If KNM-ER 1470 had indeed a derived brain, taxic diversity as a source of variation cannot be discarded.
source: If KNM-ER 1470 had indeed a derived brain, taxic diversity as a source of variation cannot be discarded.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed differences.

claim: The similarities between KNM-ER 3732 and Australopithecus sediba could be an argument supporting the presence of Australopithecus in Koobi Fora.
source: If we go further down that route, the similarities between KNM-ER 3732 and Australopithecus sediba suggested by our study could be an argument supporting the presence of Australopithecus in Koobi Fora or the absence of a definite threshold between the two genera based on the morphoarchitecture of their endocasts (Wood and Collard, 1999).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed similarities.

claim: The similarities between KNM-ER 3732 and Australopithecus sediba could be an argument supporting the absence of a definite threshold between Homo and Australopithecus based on the morphoarchitecture of their endocasts.
source: If we go further down that route, the similarities between KNM-ER 3732 and Australopithecus sediba suggested by our study could be an argument supporting the presence of Australopithecus in Koobi Fora or the absence of a definite threshold between the two genera based on the morphoarchitecture of their endocasts (Wood and Collard, 1999).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed similarities and supported by citation to Wood and Collard, 1999.

claim: Variation detected in Koobi Fora could provide information about underlying evolutionary mechanisms.
source: Beyond the taxonomic aspect, variation detected in Koobi Fora could provide information about underlying evolutionary mechanisms, and more specifically the process of fixation of an adaptive variant, i.e. a new organization of the Broca's area and the increase of neural interconnectivity in this region (Essen, 1997).
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the implications of the observed variation.

claim: A new organization of the Broca's area and the increase of neural interconnectivity in this region is an adaptive variant.
source: Beyond the taxonomic aspect, variation detected in Koobi Fora could provide information about underlying evolutionary mechanisms, and more specifically the process of fixation of an adaptive variant, i.e. a new organization of the Broca's area and the increase of neural interconnectivity in this region (Essen, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Essen, 1997.

claim: Neurological changes in the Broca's area might have had deep implications for the emergence of novel behaviors, such as articulated language.
source: Such neurological changes might have had deep implications for the emergence of novel behaviors, such as articulated language (Beaudet, 2017; Beaudet, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Beaudet, 2017 and Beaudet, 2021.

claim: The study from Ponce de León et al., 2021 would suggest that the trait of a new Broca's area organization became stabilized by 1.5 million years ago.
source: Within this scenario, the study from Ponce de León et al., 2021 would suggest that this trait became stabilized by 1.5 million years ago.
evidence: This is an inference based on the work of Ponce de León et al., 2021.

claim: Protracted brain growth has been identified as early as in Australopithecus afarensis.
source: The identification of protracted brain growth as early as in Australopithecus afarensis (Gunz et al., 2020), inducing longer exposure to the social environment during brain maturation (rev. in Hublin et al., 2015), could be consistent with a derived organization of the Broca's area being selected as a response to social environmental stimuli through developmental plasticity, culminating in this variant becoming dominant within Homo.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gunz et al., 2020.

claim: Protracted brain growth induces longer exposure to the social environment during brain maturation.
source: The identification of protracted brain growth as early as in Australopithecus afarensis (Gunz et al., 2020), inducing longer exposure to the social environment during brain maturation (rev. in Hublin et al., 2015), could be consistent with a derived organization of the Broca's area being selected as a response to social environmental stimuli through developmental plasticity, culminating in this variant becoming dominant within Homo.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hublin et al., 2015.

claim: A derived organization of the Broca's area could have been selected as a response to social environmental stimuli through developmental plasticity.
source: The identification of protracted brain growth as early as in Australopithecus afarensis (Gunz et al., 2020), inducing longer exposure to the social environment during brain maturation (rev. in Hublin et al., 2015), could be consistent with a derived organization of the Broca's area being selected as a response to social environmental stimuli through developmental plasticity, culminating in this variant becoming dominant within Homo.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about evolutionary mechanisms.

claim: The possibility of allometric scaling and the influence of brain size on sulcal patterns in early Homo has to be further explored.
source: In parallel, the possibility of allometric scaling and the influence of brain size on sulcal patterns in early Homo has to be further explored.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: KNM-ER 3732 is currently housed in the National Museums of Kenya in Nairobi (Kenya).
source: KNM-ER 3732 is currently housed in the National Museums of Kenya in Nairobi (Kenya).
evidence: This is factual information about the specimen's location.

source: We used brain and endocast atlases published in Connolly, 1950, Falk et al., 2018, and de Jager et al., 2019; de Jager et al., 2022; see also https://www.endomap.org/ for comparing the pattern identified in KNM-ER 3732 to those described in extant humans and chimpanzees.

source: In Figure 2, the extant human and chimpanzee conditions are illustrated by one extant human (adult female) and one extant chimpanzee (adult female) specimens from the Pretoria Bone Collection at the University of Pretoria (South Africa) and from the Royal Museum for Central Africa in Tervuren (Belgium), respectively (Beaudet et al., 2018).

claim: The extant chimpanzee condition in Figure 2 is illustrated by an adult female specimen from the Royal Museum for Central Africa in Tervuren (Belgium).

source: Sulcal imprints were automatically detected through a geometry-based method using curvature lines computed from the natural endocast and the inner surface of the cranium.

claim: Sulcal imprints, considered as variation points of the surface on a triangle mesh, were detected through a geometry-based method using curvature lines defined as salient subsets of the extrema of the principal curvatures on surfaces.
source: Sulcal imprints, considered as variation points of the surface on a triangle mesh, were detected through a geometry-based method using curvature lines defined as salient subsets of the extrema of the principal curvatures on surfaces (Yoshizawa et al., 2008; Beaudet et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the methodology for detecting sulcal imprints and is supported by citations.

claim: Vascular imprints and non-anatomical structures (e.g. fractures) were manually removed through a customized script written in MATLAB R2013a.
source: Vascular imprints and non-anatomical structures (e.g. fractures) were manually removed through a customized script written in MATLAB R2013a (Mathworks) that is available online (Dumoncel, 2019; https://gitlab.com/jeandumoncel/curve-editor).
evidence: This describes the methodology for data processing.
